I'll start by fixing the geometry model in my head and checking the build123d API I need.

**Model:** the leak gap is the set of points within 0.2 mm of the neck's threaded surface (dilation distributes over the union: neck = core cylinder ∪ helical ridge). So `gap = (L − N) ∩ slab(0 ≤ z ≤ 12)` where `N` = cyl(r19) ∪ ridge, `L` = cyl(r19.2) ∪ ridge offset 0.2 on every flank. Cut ends give the inner (jar side, z=0) and outer (air, z=12) openings.

```python
import build123d as bd, inspect, numpy as np
print(bd.__version__ if hasattr(bd,'__version__') else 'n/a')
print(inspect.signature(bd.Helix.__init__))
print(inspect.signature(bd.sweep))
print([m for m in dir(bd.Solid) if 'inside' in m.lower() or 'distance' in m.lower()])
```
I'll send that as an actual cell.
Now the profile geometry, computed analytically and printed against the requested numbers.
Radii check out (20.000 / 20.200). Now assemble N, L and the gap.
One solid, volume 524 mm³ ≈ (neck surface area ≈2600 mm²)×0.2. Now look at the 22 faces before classifying them.
Face centres can lie off a helical face, so I'll classify using a point actually on each face, by its distance to the neck solid N (0 → neck side, 0.2 → lid side).
Clean split: dN=0.200 exactly on the lid-side faces — a direct measurement of the 0.2 mm clearance. Now scale to metres and classify on the scaled solid with the same rule.
Patch areas match the analytic neck surface area (2601 mm²). Export one STL per patch, fine tolerance relative to the 0.2 mm gap.
Now look at it: render the four patch STLs, plus a cut view.
Geometry looks right: 6 thread turns over 12 mm, thin 0.2 mm shell. Now export STEP in metres and import into gmsh, matching gmsh surfaces to my named faces by bounding box.
Gmsh bboxes for the B-spline faces are the control-hull, not usable. I'll classify gmsh surfaces directly by a point on each surface with the same distance-to-N test, then mesh coarse immediately.
Same 10/10/1/1 split as the CAD-side classification. Physical groups, then a coarse tet mesh.
Coarse mesh exists (212k tets, volume matches). Convert to OpenFOAM now.
Mesh OK, volume matches CAD exactly. Quality is mediocre (max non-ortho 87°) because the gap is barely one cell thick; refine so there are ~2–3 cells across the 0.2 mm gap.
Two highly skew faces fail the check. Try gmsh's Netgen optimiser on the existing mesh to remove the slivers.
Mesh OK at 1.5M tets. Now a final verification: patch list, and a render of the actual volume mesh.
The slice landed on the clip plane. Let me instead zoom on an axial cross-section of the volume mesh to count cells across the 0.2 mm gap.
Quantitative check of pitch and depth straight from the meshed neck_flank patch (points in the y=0 half-plane).
The clustering loop aliased `cur` — fix it, and measure the gap honestly from lid_flank mesh points to the neck solid.
Both numbers look wrong: pyvista points are float32 numpy scalars, and the crest cluster threshold was too tight. Retest with plain floats.
Confirmed — `bd.Vector(*np_float32)` silently produced garbage; with plain floats the gap measures 0.19998 mm. Redo both measurements properly.
Sparse y=0 sampling makes band-clustering noisy. Better global test: every crest point should satisfy z − (p/2π)·θ = const (mod p) for a single-start helix of pitch p.
